title: His name is John (Luke 1:57–80)
hookLine: Zechariah's tongue loosens into a song: the dayspring from on high

lines: EIGHT DAYS: A HOUSE FULL OF OPINIONS.
cards: Eight days after the baby is born, the house is full: neighbors, cousins, the whole family, there for the circumcision and the naming. Everyone agrees: name him Zechariah, after his father.
Then Elisabeth speaks up: "Not so; but he shall be called John." The relatives push back. Nobody in your family has that name.
So they turn to the father, still silent after all these months, and make signs to ask him. And the old priest who couldn't say a word asks for a writing tablet.

teach.h: A TABLET: HIS NAME IS JOHN.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "he asked for a writing table, and wrote, saying, His name is John. And they marvelled all." Not his name will be John. His name is John: the angel settled it months ago.
In that moment of trust, "his mouth was opened immediately, and his tongue loosed, and he spake, and praised God." After months of silence, out comes praise, then a song.

In Latin it begins Benedictus, blessed: "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel; for he hath visited and redeemed his people." The first half is about all Israel, God keeping old promises to Abraham and David.

teach.h: THOU, CHILD: PROPHET OF THE HIGHEST.
teach.b: Then the old man turns to the child, and the song turns tender: "And thou, child, shalt be called the prophet of the Highest: for thou shalt go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways."

Eight days old, and hearing your job description. Then: "whereby the dayspring from on high hath visited us, To give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace."
Dayspring is an old English word for sunrise. Christians hear in it Jesus, the light John will point toward.

teach.h: THE DAYSPRING FROM ON HIGH HATH VISITED US.
teach.b: Behind it is the Greek anatole, a rising, and some readers notice the old Greek version of the prophets uses the same word for the promised branch from David's line. A sunrise, and a new shoot from an old tree.
In Catholic Lauds and Anglican and Lutheran Morning Prayer, Zechariah's song is still prayed or sung at the hour the dayspring comes.

how: The Benedictus is sung or said each morning in several traditions: at Lauds in the Catholic Liturgy of the Hours and at Morning Prayer in Anglican and Lutheran traditions.

o: Zechariah's song, named for its first Latin word, blessed
the Latin word for the writing tablet Zechariah asked for

games.q: what's inside Luke 1:57–80 — tap the pairs.
p: not so; he shall be called John

s: Zechariah wrote "his name will be John"
he wrote "his name is John": already settled.
Zechariah's first words after his silence were a song
his tongue was loosed, and he praised God.
it's Latin for blessed, the song's first word.

games.q: you're Zechariah, still unable to speak. the whole family wants to name your son after you. they turn to you. what do you do?
o: ask for a tablet and write: his name is John.
leave the choice to the relatives.
games.why: he writes "his name is John," and at once his mouth is opened, and his first words in months are praise.

practice: If it's morning, face the light; if not, picture tomorrow's sunrise, the sky going gray, then pale, then gold at the edge.
Think of the darkness Zechariah sings about, the shadow someone you know, or you, may be sitting in, and let the light come up slowly in your mind, a little at a time.
If you pray, greet the morning with Zechariah's words, light to them that sit in darkness; if not, watch the light arrive.

wordCard.voice: Benedictus. Latin for blessed, the first word of Zechariah's song when his tongue is loosed, still sung in morning prayer.

orig.note: Greek: a rising, sunrise, the east. the dayspring of Zechariah's song.

carryVoice: Your line: the dayspring from on high. Light, a little at a time. That's day five hundred seven.
